guide.beliefs: A deliberately built value system from Malcolm and Simone Collins, authors of the Pragmatist's Guide books. They describe it as an iteration of Puritan Christianity rebuilt for a technological age, held with a secular, evidence-minded outlook. Families should consciously choose and hand down their own culture (their word is a "cultivar"); the point of a life is measured by the descendants and the lasting culture it leaves (their "descendant worship"); and humanity's purpose is to keep growing in diverse complexity and spread outward.
guide.values: Having children and raising them well; hard work, grit and "cunning" over raw talent; self-control built through deliberate self-denial (fasting, Sabbath-style practices); thrift and asceticism over consumption; embracing technology, including reproductive technology and AI; many distinct family and religious cultures coexisting rather than one universal culture.
guide.forbids: Self-indulgent hedonism and luxury; idleness; consumerism; giving up on having a family; anti-technology retreat. They are sharply critical of what they call a "cultural supervirus" in mainstream elite culture, which they link to parts of the social justice movement and academia, and blame for falling birth rates.
guide.family: Large families and many children are central; parents are expected to raise children deliberately inside a chosen family culture (a "House"), with traditions, a family name and a governance of its own. They support embryo screening and other reproductive technology.
guide.stories: Stories are judged by what they teach: whether discipline, sacrifice and building something for the next generation are rewarded, whether technology and science improve human life, and whether pleasure-seeking or despair are shown as empty. They are not especially troubled by intense content itself.
guide.range: A new, small movement centered on the Collins family and their followers (Based Camp podcast, technopuritan.com); views are still being written down in their "tracts". Widely debated, especially its pronatalism, embryo selection and parenting views.
guide.sources: Malcolm and Simone Collins, The Pragmatist's Guide to Crafting Religion, to Life, to Governance, to Relationships and to Sexuality; the Techno-Puritan tracts on the Based Camp podcast and technopuritan.com

topics.Alcohol: No ban; the authors drink and treat it as a known risk. They note that many religions' prohibitions protect people from hazards like alcohol, so a family may set its own rule.
topics.Tobacco and drugs: Addiction is treated as a threat to self-control and to the values a family sets; warning children away from drugs is described as a parent's job.
topics.Magic, occult and spirits: Approaches the world through science and technology; fantasy magic is not a concern in itself, but superstition presented as truth runs against its evidence-minded outlook.
topics.Other religions and gods shown: Pluralist: many distinct religious and family cultures should coexist and compete; respectful portrayals of other faiths are not a concern.
topics.Violence, war and revenge: Judged by what the story rewards; hardship, competition and sacrifice for one's people are respected, cruelty for its own sake is not.
topics.Sexuality, nudity and modesty: Frank and analytical about sex (The Pragmatist's Guide to Sexuality). The concern is not depiction but sex treated as pure pleasure-seeking cut off from commitment and family.
topics.Same-sex relationships and gender identi: Discussed openly and without condemnation in the books; the emphasis is on building a committed family and raising children rather than on rules about orientation.
topics.Gender roles and family: Family is central: committed couples running their household as a team (their "NeoCorp" family model), many children, and a deliberately chosen family culture. Each family sets its own roles.
topics.Language and blasphemy: Not a focus of the tradition.
topics.Authority, parents and rebellion: Parents are expected to pass down a deliberate culture; rebellion that rejects family-building or discipline is a concern, but children are expected to choose their own path in the end.
topics.Death, afterlife and suicide: Meaning comes from what you leave to descendants and the future; despair and stories that treat life as pointless run against it.
topics.Lying and deception: Values honest reasoning and updating beliefs on evidence; deception shown as clever without cost is a mild concern.

guide.media: Judges a story mainly by its message about family, discipline and progress rather than by intensity.
guide.note: Grades for this tradition are estimated, not written series by series: each one is worked out from the guide's existing analysis of the story's main ideas. A story gains when it affirms practical problem-solving, discipline and virtue, self-control, family duty, tradition, progress or helpful technology, and loses when it affirms pleasure-seeking, anti-natalism, nihilism, consumerism or self-expression as the goal of life (critiquing those counts in its favor).
